knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inequality systems \(A\theta\leq b\) and \(C\theta\leq d\) are equivalent polyhedral representations when \[\{\theta\in\mathbb R^p:A\theta\leq b\}=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^p:C\theta\leq d\}.\] Equivalently, every inequality in \(C\theta\leq d\) is valid for the first polyhedron and every inequality in \(A\theta\leq b\) is valid for the second. Equivalent descriptions may have different numbers of inequalities, positive row scalings, or redundant rows. In multiparametric QP, replacing one by another preserves the critical parameter set and any optimizer formula valid on that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two polyhedral representations are equivalent when they define exactly the same parameter set, even if their inequalities, row counts, or redundancies differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Polyhedral Representations

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Region Redundancy
children.top_down_role: Region-description redundancy attributable to nonunique active-set or multiplier representations.

assumptions_latex: The multiparametric convex QP has affine parameter dependence and a polyhedral feasible set.
Each candidate active set defines a polyhedral parameter set through its KKT feasibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy may therefore make the active-set-indexed critical-region representation nonminimal even when the represented primal solution map is unchanged.

notation.meaning: KKT-feasible parameter region associated with active set I
primal optimizer law associated with active set I

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports degeneracy-induced redundancy in multiparametric QP region representations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-set descriptions of polyhedral parameter regions, including overlap caused by primal or dual degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_I\) and \(R_J\) be KKT-feasible parameter regions generated by distinct active sets \(I\neq J\). Degeneracy-induced region redundancy occurs when \(\operatorname{relint}(R_I\cap R_J)\neq\varnothing\) and \(x_I(\theta)=x_J(\theta)\) throughout \(R_I\cap R_J\), while the associated active sets, multiplier selections, or KKT bases differ. A description \(R_I\) is removable from a family \(\{R_K\}_{K\in\mathcal K}\) when \(R_I\subseteq\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal K\setminus\{I\}}R_K\) and every covering region supplies the same primal optimizer on its overlap with \(R_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy can assign different active sets or multiplier bases to overlapping parameter regions with the same optimizer law, making the region family nonminimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Region Redundancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the degeneracy-induced region-redundancy leaf and its notation is internally consistent, but no cited source with an inspectable locator supports the overlap or removability characterization.

children.title: Set-Valued Parametric Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Nonunique parametric solutions under singular curvature.

assumptions_latex: For every parameter under consideration, the feasible set is nonempty and the convex quadratic objective attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution map is set-valued exactly at parameters for which \(S(\theta)\) contains more than one point; singular curvature can make such a set an optimal face.

notation.meaning: set of primal minimizers at parameter theta

review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats set-valued solution maps for singular multiparametric convex QPs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex QPs whose positive-semidefinite Hessian need not be positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(H\succeq0\), parameter-dependent vector \(c(\theta)\), and polyhedron \(X(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the parametric primal solution map is
\[S(\theta):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X(\theta)}\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}x\right\}.\]
It is a set-valued map from the parameter domain into subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\). If \(x_1,x_2\in S(\theta)\), convexity implies \([x_1,x_2]\subseteq S(\theta)\); moreover, for \(d=x_2-x_1\), one has \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\). Thus singular curvature permits positive-dimensional optimal faces and precludes an intrinsically single-valued local sensitivity map without an additional selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution map assigns each parameter its entire convex set of QP minimizers; singular curvature may produce positive-dimensional optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Parametric Solution Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this leaf, and the argmin map and zero-curvature conclusion are standard. However, no source is cited, and a convex QP minimizer set need not be a face of the feasible polyhedron, so the repeated claim that singular curvature produces an 'optimal face' requires correction or precise qualification before sourcing.

children.title: Critical-Region Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial growth in the number of distinct active-face regions.

assumptions_latex: The multiparametric QP has \(m\) inequalities and affine parameter dependence.
A critical region is indexed by the optimizer's active inequality set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of distinct active-set regions is at most \(2^m\), or at most \(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{m}{k}\) when only independent active sets of size at most \(n\) are admitted.

notation.meaning: number of distinct nonempty active-set regions

review_flags: The combinatorial bound is standard counting, but the supplied sources do not directly document critical-region complexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial bounds for active-set-indexed regions; representation duplicates are excluded from the count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every parameter with an optimizer determines an active subset \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). For a fixed active set whose KKT system determines an affine primal-dual law, primal feasibility and multiplier nonnegativity define at most one convex polyhedral parameter region. Consequently,
\[N_{\mathrm{cr}}\leq 2^m.\]
If every retained active set has linearly independent active normals in \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(|I|\leq n\) and
\[N_{\mathrm{cr}}\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\min\{m,n\}}\binom{m}{k}.\]
These are worst-case enumeration bounds; degeneracy can create multiple descriptions of one geometric region but does not increase the number of possible active subsets beyond \(2^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Critical regions can proliferate combinatorially: at most one per active subset, hence at most two to the power of the number of inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Proliferation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the proliferation leaf. The counting bounds are plausible under the stated active-set indexing and unique-law qualification, but no source with a specific locator supports their application to multiparametric-QP critical regions.

children.title: Parametric-Solution Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Downstream uses of local derivatives and globally precomputed critical-region representations.

children.title: Critical-Region Point Location
children.top_down_role: Online location of a parameter query within a precomputed region partition.

assumptions_latex: A finite family of closed polyhedra covers the admissible parameter domain.
Each region is stored by linear inequalities and carries its associated solution law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a region containing the query and its associated optimizer value, or reports that the query lies outside the represented domain.

notation.meaning: affine solution law on region j

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports point-location algorithms for explicit multiparametric QP partitions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic online lookup in a precomputed finite critical-region cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a query \(\bar\theta\) and stored data \(\{(H_j,h_j,K_j,k_j)\}_{j=1}^N\). For \(j=1,\ldots,N\), test the componentwise inequalities \(H_j\bar\theta\leq h_j\). Stop at the first successful index and output \(j\) together with \(K_j\bar\theta+k_j\). If several regions contain a boundary query, use the smallest successful index; consistency requires their optimizer laws to agree at \(\bar\theta\), or a prescribed selection rule must resolve a set-valued solution. If no test succeeds, output \(\mathrm{outside}\). Exhaustive lookup uses \(O(\sum_{j=1}^N r_jp)\) scalar arithmetic and comparisons when \(H_j\) has \(r_j\) rows and \(\theta\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test a query against stored region inequalities, apply the matching affine optimizer law, and use a fixed tie rule on shared boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Point Location

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind matches the point-location interface, and the exhaustive membership procedure is coherent. A source is still required for the critical-region lookup formulation and stated arithmetic complexity.

children.title: Explicit Control-Law Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of piecewise parametric QP solutions in explicit control.

assumptions_latex: The finite-horizon constrained control problem is represented by a strictly convex multiparametric QP with state parameter \(x\).
Its critical regions cover the feasible state domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explicit feedback interface is a continuous piecewise-affine law when adjacent optimizer laws agree on every shared boundary.

notation.meaning: matrix selecting the first control move

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the explicit-control interpretation of multiparametric QP solution laws.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-move feedback extracted from an explicit finite-horizon QP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the precomputed optimizer satisfies \(U^*(x)=K_jx+k_j\) for every \(x\in R_j\), where \(\{R_j\}_{j=1}^N\) covers the feasible state domain. The explicit control-law interface returns
\[\kappa(x):=E_0U^*(x)=E_0(K_jx+k_j)\quad\text{for any }j\text{ with }x\in R_j.\]
At runtime it performs critical-region point location, evaluates the corresponding affine expression, and applies only \(\kappa(x)\). The interface is single-valued on shared boundaries precisely when \(E_0(K_ix+k_i)=E_0(K_jx+k_j)\) for every \(x\in R_i\cap R_j\); otherwise a declared selection rule is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit control locates the current state's critical region and evaluates the first component of that region's affine optimal-input law.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Control-Law Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the explicit-control interface and the first-move extraction is stated consistently. No cited source with a specific locator supports the multiparametric-QP-to-explicit-control interpretation or its boundary conditions.

children.title: Differentiable QP-Layer Interface
children.top_down_role: Derivative and adjoint access to locally regular QP solution maps.

assumptions_latex: The active set is locally constant and satisfies linear independence and strict complementarity.
The displayed KKT matrix is nonsingular at the parameter of interest.
Only the linear objective and constraint right-hand sides depend differentiably on the parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A forward derivative or reverse-mode adjoint is obtained by one solve with the KKT matrix or its transpose.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports implicit differentiation and adjoints for a regular QP layer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local implicit differentiation with a fixed active set and nonsingular KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the QP with objective \(\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}Hz+q(\theta)^{\mathsf T}z\), equalities \(Az=b(\theta)\), and inequalities \(Gz\leq h(\theta)\), form
\[M_I:=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&G_I^{\mathsf T}\\A&0&0\\G_I&0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_I:=\begin{bmatrix}-Dq(\theta)\\Db(\theta)\\Dh_I(\theta)\end{bmatrix}.\]
Given a direction \(v\), solve \(M_Iw=B_Iv\); the primal block of \(w\) is \(Dz(\theta)v\). Given an output cotangent \(\bar z\), solve \(M_I^{\mathsf T}a=(\bar z,0,0)\) and return \(B_I^{\mathsf T}a\). Loss of the assumptions invalidates this classical derivative interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed regular active set, forward sensitivities and reverse-mode gradients follow from solves with the local KKT matrix and its transpose.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable QP-Layer Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is suitable for derivative and adjoint access. The fixed-active-set KKT differentiation formulas are internally consistent, but they require an authoritative source with a specific locator covering the regularity assumptions and forward/reverse solves.

children.title: Convex QP Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: The principal boundaries where standard uniqueness, sensitivity, certificate, or convex-QP conclusions fail or leave the chapter's scope.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 16.1 and 16.4: equality-constrained properties and degeneracy

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Bonnans and Shapiro, Perturbation Analysis of Optimization Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Bonnans and Shapiro, Perturbation Analysis of Optimization Problems

children.title: Loss of Primal-Dual Regularity
children.top_down_role: Failures arising from singular reduced curvature, dependent activity, or weak complementarity.

children.title: Nonunique Primal Solutions
children.top_down_role: Positive-dimensional optimal sets and set-valued local sensitivity.

assumptions_latex: The QP minimizes \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) over a convex polyhedron, with \(H\succeq0\).
Two distinct feasible points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal set contains the nontrivial segment \([x_1,x_2]\), so the primal solution is nonunique and ordinary single-valued sensitivity is unavailable.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not directly locate the stated characterization of nonunique solutions in convex QPs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-dimensional optimal sets caused by zero curvature along feasible optimal directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexity gives \((1-t)x_1+tx_2\in X^*\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Because both endpoints minimize the quadratic, its restriction to their segment is constant, which forces
\[d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\quad\text{and hence}\quad Hd=0.\]
Thus nonuniqueness can occur only along a zero-curvature direction of \(H\). Conversely, if an optimizer \(x^*\) admits a nonzero direction \(d\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(x^*+td\) is feasible for \(t\in[0,\varepsilon]\), \(Hd=0\), and \((Hx^*+c)^{\mathsf T}d=0\), then the entire segment \(\{x^*+td:0\leq t\leq\varepsilon\}\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct minimizers force a zero-curvature direction and an optimal segment; conversely, a feasible stationary zero-curvature segment consists entirely of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Primal Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the zero-curvature segment characterization is mathematically coherent for a positive-semidefinite quadratic. No cited source with an inspectable locator supports the stated necessary and sufficient conditions.

children.title: Nonunique Multipliers
children.top_down_role: Dual ambiguity caused by dependent active constraints.

assumptions_latex: A primal optimizer \(x^*\) satisfies the convex-QP KKT conditions.
The active constraint-normal matrix is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multipliers are nonunique whenever the affine stationarity nullspace contains a nonzero direction that preserves multiplier nonnegativity.

notation.meaning: active inequality index set at the optimizer

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports multiplier nonuniqueness under dependent active constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual ambiguity at a fixed primal optimizer with dependent active inequality normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x^*\), active multipliers satisfy
\[G_I^{\mathsf T}\lambda_I=-(Hx^*+c+A^{\mathsf T}\nu),\qquad \lambda_I\geq0.\]
Hence the multiplier set is the intersection of an affine space with the nonnegative orthant. If a feasible multiplier \(\lambda_I\) and a nonzero vector \(d\in\ker(G_I^{\mathsf T})\) admit distinct scalars \(t_1\neq t_2\) such that \(\lambda_I+t_kd\geq0\) for \(k=1,2\), then both \(\lambda_I+t_1d\) and \(\lambda_I+t_2d\) satisfy stationarity, dual feasibility, and complementarity. The primal optimizer may remain unique even though its multipliers are not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent active normals create dual ambiguity when a stationarity-null direction permits multiple nonnegative multiplier vectors at the same primal optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Multipliers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits dual ambiguity. The conditional nullspace construction is coherent, but the role attributes ambiguity to dependent active constraints while the displayed test varies only inequality multipliers and holds equality multipliers fixed; a source should establish the intended scope and full active-gradient formulation.

children.title: Failure of Strict Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Weakly active constraints and unstable primal-dual face identification.

assumptions_latex: For inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), a KKT pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict complementarity fails exactly when some active constraint has zero multiplier; such a constraint is weakly active and cannot be identified from multiplier sign alone.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports strict-complementarity failure and weak activity for convex QPs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weakly active inequalities at a convex-QP KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Strict complementarity requires
\[g_i(x^*)<0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_i^*=0,\qquad g_i(x^*)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_i^*>0.\]
Its failure is the existence of \(i\) with \(g_i(x^*)=0\) and \(\lambda_i^*=0\). For example, consider \(\min_x\tfrac12x^2+\theta x\) subject to \(-x\leq0\). At \(\theta=0\), the unique optimizer is \(x^*=0\) and the multiplier is \(0\), so the bound is weakly active. For \(\theta<0\) the optimizer is interior, whereas for \(\theta>0\) the bound is active with positive multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity fails when an active inequality has zero multiplier, allowing small parameter changes to switch whether that constraint remains active.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Strict Complementarity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and weak-activity definition fit the leaf, and the scalar example is consistent. No source with a specific locator supports the strict-complementarity terminology or the claimed identification instability.

children.title: Sensitivity Breakdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Loss of smooth, Lipschitz, or single-valued parameter dependence.

children.title: Active-Face Bifurcation
children.top_down_role: Parameter values where competing active-face regimes meet.

assumptions_latex: Consider the scalar parametric convex QP \(\min_x\tfrac12x^2+\theta x\) subject to \(x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameter \(\theta=0\) is an active-face bifurcation: the interior and boundary regimes meet there, and strict complementarity fails.
review_flags: The concrete example is directly checkable, but no supplied source locator addresses active-face bifurcation terminology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar model of two neighboring active-face regimes meeting at a weakly active parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unique primal-dual solution is
\[(x^*(\theta),\lambda^*(\theta))=\begin{cases}(-\theta,0),&\theta<0,\\(0,\theta),&\theta\geq0.\end{cases}\]
Thus the optimizer lies in the interior face \(x>0\) for \(\theta<0\) and on the boundary face \(x=0\) for \(\theta>0\). At \(\theta=0\), both regime closures meet and \(x^*(0)=\lambda^*(0)=0\). The active constraint is weakly active at this parameter, so the locally valid active face changes under arbitrarily small perturbations of opposite sign, even though the primal solution remains continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero, an interior optimizer regime and a boundary-active regime meet; arbitrarily small parameter changes select different active faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Face Bifurcation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counter-regime calculation is correct and a failure boundary is the appropriate role. The term 'active-face bifurcation' and its interpretation are not supported by any cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Loss of Solution-Map Lipschitzness
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by failed rank, curvature, or complementarity regularity.

assumptions_latex: Consider the parametric convex QP with zero objective, bounds \(-1\leq x\leq1\), and equality \(\theta x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution map is not locally Lipschitz at \(\theta=0\) in Hausdorff distance because its distance from \(S(0)\) remains \(1\) for every nonzero nearby parameter.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance between nonempty compact sets

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this counterexample or Hausdorff-Lipschitz sensitivity failure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete set-valued sensitivity failure when constraint rank changes at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because every feasible point is optimal, the solution map is
\[S(\theta)=\begin{cases}[-1,1],&\theta=0,\\\{0\},&\theta\neq0.\end{cases}\]
For every \(\theta\neq0\), one has \(d_H(S(\theta),S(0))=1\). Therefore no neighborhood of zero and no finite constant \(L\) can satisfy \(d_H(S(\theta),S(0))\leq L|\theta|\). The failure is caused by loss of rank of the equality coefficient at \(\theta=0\), which enlarges the feasible and optimal set discontinuously. This example concerns the full set-valued solution map, not an arbitrarily chosen single-valued selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an equality loses rank, the optimal set can jump from a singleton to an interval, violating every local Hausdorff-Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Solution-Map Lipschitzness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits this failure leaf, and the displayed solution map and Hausdorff-distance calculation are internally consistent. A source is required for the set-valued Lipschitz notion and the interpretation as a QP sensitivity failure.

children.title: Multiplier Discontinuity
children.top_down_role: Abrupt dual behavior near degenerate active faces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique multipliers on the two sides of \(\theta=0\) have different limits, so no multiplier selection is continuous through the degenerate parameter.
review_flags: The concrete example is directly checkable, but no supplied locator documents multiplier discontinuity at a degenerate active face.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar QP whose duplicate active bounds cause incompatible one-sided multiplier limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\theta<0\), only the second bound is active and
\[x^*(\theta)=\theta,\qquad (\lambda_1^*(\theta),\lambda_2^*(\theta))=(0,1-\theta).\]
For \(\theta>0\), only the first bound is active and
\[x^*(\theta)=0,\qquad (\lambda_1^*(\theta),\lambda_2^*(\theta))=(1,0).\]
At \(\theta=0\), the two bounds coincide and the multiplier set is \(\{(a,1-a):0\leq a\leq1\}\). The left multiplier limit is \((0,1)\), while the right limit is \((1,0)\). Hence every multiplier selection agreeing with the unique neighboring multipliers is discontinuous at zero, although the primal optimizer is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coincident active bounds create nonunique multipliers at zero, while the unique multipliers on either side converge to different vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Discontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the multiplier-discontinuity leaf, and the primal and multiplier formulas are consistent. No cited source with a specific locator supports this example or the asserted degeneracy-based discontinuity phenomenon.

children.title: Numerical Certificate Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision regimes in which residuals and statuses require conditioning-aware interpretation.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned KKT Systems
children.top_down_role: Loss of numerical reliability near rank or curvature singularity.

assumptions_latex: The fixed-active-set convex QP has the nonsingular KKT matrix \(K=\begin{bmatrix}Q&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\), where \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\frac{\|\Delta z\|_2}{\|z\|_2}\le \frac{\kappa_2(K)}{1-\|K^{-1}\|_2\|\Delta K\|_2}\left(\frac{\|\Delta K\|_2}{\|K\|_2}+\frac{\|\Delta d\|_2}{\|d\|_2}\right).\] Consequently, the perturbation bound deteriorates as \(\sigma_{\min}(K)\) approaches zero.

notation.meaning: stacked primal-dual solution and KKT right-hand side

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained or fixed-active-set convex QPs with sufficiently small finite-dimensional perturbations.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Approximation Procedures for Nondifferentiable and Ill-Conditioned Optimization Problems p. 167
source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Kz=d\) and \((K+\Delta K)(z+\Delta z)=d+\Delta d\). If \(K\) is nonsingular, \(z\ne0\), \(d\ne0\), and \(\|K^{-1}\|_2\|\Delta K\|_2<1\), then \[\frac{\|\Delta z\|_2}{\|z\|_2}\le \frac{\kappa_2(K)}{1-\|K^{-1}\|_2\|\Delta K\|_2}\left(\frac{\|\Delta K\|_2}{\|K\|_2}+\frac{\|\Delta d\|_2}{\|d\|_2}\right),\qquad \kappa_2(K)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(K)}{\sigma_{\min}(K)}.\] Thus near rank loss, perturbations and residual errors can be strongly amplified, limiting the numerical reliability of the computed primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsingular fixed-active-set KKT system under a sufficiently small matrix perturbation, relative solution error is bounded by a factor involving the KKT condition number. Reliability therefore deteriorates near rank loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned KKT Systems

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Approximation Procedures for Nondifferentiable and Ill-Conditioned Optimization Problems p. 167
source_witnesses.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

children.title: Numerical Status Ambiguity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Difficulty separating small residuals from mathematically decisive status evidence.

children.title: Near-Infeasible Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances lying close to the boundary between feasible status plus infeasible status.

assumptions_latex: A parameterized QP has feasible-parameter set \(\Theta_F=\{\theta:F(\theta)\ne\varnothing\}\).
The parameter norm and data representation are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\Theta\setminus\Theta_F)\le\varepsilon\), perturbations of size \(\varepsilon\) can change feasibility status.

notation.meaning: distance to the infeasible parameter region

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distance to the feasibility boundary formalizes near-infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-space boundary, with distance measured in the chosen data norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[d_F(\theta):=\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\Theta\setminus\Theta_F).\] A feasible parameter \(\theta\in\Theta_F\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible when \(d_F(\theta)\le\varepsilon\). Then there exists an infeasible \(\widehat\theta\) with \(\|\widehat\theta-\theta\|\le\varepsilon+\eta\) for every \(\eta>0\). Consequently, data uncertainty or backward error of this scale can cross the feasibility boundary, so feasibility classification is not robust without a positive lower bound on \(d_F(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is near-infeasible when its parameter lies close to the infeasible region; perturbations at that scale can reverse the true feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Infeasible Parameter Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance-to-infeasibility formulation is precise and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no inspectable source supports this parameter-space robustness statement.

children.title: Weak Numerical Certificates
children.top_down_role: Status evidence whose numerical strength is insufficient for decisive interpretation.

assumptions_latex: A computed primal-dual point has aggregate KKT residual \(R(z;d)\).
The exact solution map is locally regular only with modulus \(\gamma(d)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication \(R(z;d)\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*(d))\le C\varepsilon\) requires a finite error-bound constant \(C\); residual size alone is insufficient.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual certificates require conditioning-dependent error bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate KKT certificates for convex QPs near degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A residual certificate \(R(z;d)\le\varepsilon\) is weak unless an error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*(d))\le\gamma(d)^{-1}R(z;d)\] is known with \(\gamma(d)\) bounded away from zero. Along data sequences for which \(\gamma(d_k)\downarrow0\), points may satisfy \(R(z_k;d_k)\to0\) while their distance from \(Z^*(d_k)\) decreases arbitrarily slowly or remains uncontrolled. Thus a small reported KKT residual alone does not certify a comparably accurate primal-dual solution near singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small KKT residual is a weak certificate when no stable error bound converts residual size into distance from an exact primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Numerical Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly identifies a conditioning-dependent error-bound boundary, but the asserted behavior along vanishing regularity moduli needs a source specifying the applicable QP error-bound or metric-regularity hypotheses.

children.title: Residual-Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Cases where small residuals do not reliably distinguish competing mathematical statuses.

assumptions_latex: For \(\delta\in\mathbb R\), consider the scalar QP with constraints \(x\le0\) and \(x\ge\delta\).
Constraint residual is the maximum positive violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arbitrarily small residuals occur for both feasible instances \(\delta\le0\) and infeasible instances \(\delta>0\), so residual magnitude alone does not determine status.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary QP family establishes the claim
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar convex feasibility QP demonstrating status ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[P_\delta:\quad \min_{x\in\mathbb R}0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\le0,\quad x\ge\delta,\] and define \(r_\delta(x)=\max\{x,-x+\delta,0\}\). If \(\delta\le0\), then \(P_\delta\) is feasible. If \(\delta>0\), it is infeasible, yet at \(x=\delta/2\) one has \(r_\delta(x)=\delta/2\to0\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Hence an arbitrarily small constraint residual can accompany either exact feasibility or exact infeasibility in nearby instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a scalar family, feasible and infeasible instances approach the same boundary while both admit arbitrarily small constraint residuals; residual size cannot identify status.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Status Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar construction and residual calculation are internally correct, and counterexample is the exact mathematical role for this leaf. The record nevertheless has no cited source, as already reflected by its needs_source status.

children.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Status conclusions that change materially under plausible numerical tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The scalar family \(P_\delta\) has constraints \(x\le0\) and \(x\ge\delta\).
A numerical classifier accepts feasibility when some tested point has violation at most \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0<\delta\le2\tau\), the infeasible problem passes the residual test at \(x=\delta/2\); reducing \(\tau\) below \(\delta/2\) reverses the classification.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute feasibility tolerance in a scalar convex QP family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P_\delta\), define \(r_\delta(x)=\max\{x,-x+\delta,0\}\). When \(\delta>0\), the exact problem is infeasible and \[\inf_x r_\delta(x)=r_\delta(\delta/2)=\delta/2.\] A rule declaring numerical feasibility whenever \(r_\delta(x)\le\tau\) therefore accepts this infeasible instance if \(\tau\ge\delta/2\), but rejects it if \(\tau<\delta/2\). Thus the reported status changes with tolerance whenever the instance lies within the tolerance scale of the feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible scalar QP is classified feasible when tolerance exceeds half its constraint gap, and infeasible when tolerance is tightened below that threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Status Classification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tolerance threshold is correct for the stated scalar classifier, and counterexample fits the terminal container. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Certificate Transformation Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Certificate distortion or loss during scaling, reformulation, and presolve recovery.

children.title: Scaling-Induced Certificate Distortion
children.top_down_role: Changes in certificate magnitude or interpretability caused by numerical scaling.

assumptions_latex: Original constraints are \(Ax=b\), and diagonal scalings \(D_r,D_c\) are nonsingular.
Scaled variables and equations satisfy \(x=D_c\widehat x\) and \(D_rAD_c\widehat x=D_rb\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat r=D_rr\), so \(\sigma_{\min}(D_r)\|r\|_2\le\|\widehat r\|_2\le\sigma_{\max}(D_r)\|r\|_2\); scaled residual tolerances need not preserve original certificate strength.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact residual transformation under diagonal scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal row and variable scaling of affine QP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=Ax-b\) be the original equality residual. After scaling, \[\widehat r=D_r(D_r^{-1}D_rAD_c\widehat x-b)=D_rr,\] equivalently using the scaled equation \(D_rAD_c\widehat x=D_rb\). Therefore \[\sigma_{\min}(D_r)\|r\|_2\le\|\widehat r\|_2\le\sigma_{\max}(D_r)\|r\|_2.\] If \(D_r\) is badly conditioned or has extreme magnitude, a small scaled residual may correspond to a large original residual, or conversely. Certificate tolerances must consequently be transformed with the scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row scaling multiplies constraint residuals by the scaling matrix, so extreme scaling can make the same certificate appear much stronger or weaker.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Induced Certificate Distortion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual transformation and singular-value bounds are correct for nonsingular diagonal row scaling, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A solver-scaling source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Back-Transformation Certificate Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of certificate validity or precision during recovery in the original variables.

assumptions_latex: A reformulated variable is mapped back by \(x=Tz+t\).
A computed point satisfies \(\widehat z=z+e_z\), and arithmetic adds recovery error \(e_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x-x=Te_z+e_r\), so \(\|\widehat x-x\|\le\|T\|\|e_z\|+\|e_r\|\); unstable recovery can destroy a reformulated certificate.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine error propagation gives the certificate-loss boundary
dedicated presolve or reformulation source needed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine recovery from a transformed continuous QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the exact correspondence is \(x=Tz+t\), while numerical recovery returns \(\widehat x=T\widehat z+t+e_r\) with \(\widehat z=z+e_z\). Then \[\widehat x-x=Te_z+e_r,\qquad \|\widehat x-x\|\le\|T\|\|e_z\|+\|e_r\|.\] Consequently, a small error or residual in transformed coordinates does not yield a comparably small original-space certificate when \(\|T\|\) is large or recovery incurs significant rounding. Original feasibility and KKT residuals must be recomputed after back-transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unstable or inaccurate inverse transformation can amplify transformed-solution error, so the recovered point may lose feasibility or KKT accuracy in original coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Back-Transformation Certificate Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine error-propagation bound is correct, but the broader claim about feasibility and KKT certificate loss requires a source that connects transformed-coordinate errors to original-space certificate residuals.

children.title: Presolve Recovery Failures
children.top_down_role: Certificate inconsistencies introduced while reconstructing eliminated variables or constraints.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For an original row \(A_E x_E+A_Rz=b\), recovery error contributes \(A_Ee_E\) and can invalidate the reduced certificate.

notation.meaning: constraint blocks for eliminated and retained variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: substitution exposes postsolve residual amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Postsolve reconstruction after affine variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume exact elimination gives \(x_E=Rz+s\). If postsolve uses \(\widehat x_E=R\widehat z+s+e_E\), then for an original constraint row the recovered residual is \[A_E\widehat x_E+A_R\widehat z-b=\bigl(A_ER+A_R\bigr)\widehat z+A_Es-b+A_Ee_E.\] Even when the reduced residual vanishes, the original residual equals \(A_Ee_E\). Hence inaccurate stored transformations, ill-conditioned substitutions, or inconsistent recovery can prevent a reduced-space certificate from lifting to a valid original-space certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Presolve may certify the reduced QP, yet inaccurate reconstruction of eliminated variables can reintroduce original constraint violations and invalidate postsolve certification.
knowledge_statements.title: Presolve Recovery Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The postsolve substitution identity is correct under the stated affine elimination model, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No presolve or postsolve recovery source is supplied.

children.title: Reformulation Certificate Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Disagreement between certificates for a transformed model versus the original QP.

assumptions_latex: A reformulation maps feasible points by \(x=\pi(z)\).
A certificate predicate for the original problem is \(C_P(x,y)=0\), while the reformulated predicate is \(C_R(z,w)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reformulated certificate transfers only if a computable dual map \(y=\psi(w,z)\) satisfies \(C_R(z,w)=0\Rightarrow C_P(\pi(z),\psi(w,z))=0\).

notation.meaning: primal projection from reformulated to original variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: certificate preservation requires an explicit primal-dual implication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reformulations with potentially nontrivial dual recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reformulated certificate \((z,w)\) is valid for the original QP only when there are computable maps \(x=\pi(z)\) and \(y=\psi(w,z)\) such that \[C_R(z,w)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_P\bigl(\pi(z),\psi(w,z)\bigr)=0.\] Equality of primal optimal values or projection of feasible sets alone does not establish this implication. If auxiliary constraints, duplicated variables, or altered multiplier conventions prevent construction of \(\psi\), the reformulated certificate and the claimed original-space certificate are mismatched.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent primal formulations do not automatically have equivalent certificates; primal projection and dual recovery must preserve the original certificate equations.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Certificate Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication is a reasonable abstract certificate-transfer condition, but the terminal container concerns a failure phenomenon and would be better represented as failure_boundary. A source is also needed to establish an applicable primal-dual recovery framework rather than only a predicate-level tautology.

children.title: Boundary of Convex QP Scope
children.top_down_role: Model extensions that require transfer to other chapters rather than expansion here.

children.title: Indefinite Quadratic Objectives
children.top_down_role: The transition from convex QP to nonconvex quadratic programming.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic objective is \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
For the stationary-point example, the problem is unconstrained and \(c=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Q\) has a negative eigenvalue, then \(f\) is nonconvex; in the unconstrained case with \(c=0\), \(x=0\) is stationary but is not a local minimizer.

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian of the quadratic objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from continuous convex QP to continuous nonconvex quadratic programming.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with symmetric \(Q\), the presence of a negative eigenvalue of \(Q\) makes the objective nonconvex. In the unconstrained case with \(c=0\), the stationary point \(x=0\) is not a local minimizer. Thus stationarity and the convex-QP KKT sufficiency principle do not certify local or global minimality once the quadratic objective is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative eigenvalue of the quadratic Hessian makes the objective nonconvex. In the unconstrained zero-linear-term case, the stationary origin is not a local minimum, so convex-QP sufficiency no longer applies.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic Objectives

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

children.title: Quadratically Constrained Extensions
children.top_down_role: The transition from affine-constrained QP to convex or nonconvex QCQP.

assumptions_latex: Equality constraints, if present, are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The QCQP is convex when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\); an indefinite objective or inequality Hessian generally leaves convex-QP scope.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous QCQP with quadratic inequalities and affine equalities.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad Ax=b,\] where \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\). It is a convex QCQP when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\), because the objective and inequality functions are convex and the equalities are affine. Allowing an indefinite \(Q_i\) generally produces a nonconvex feasible set or objective and leaves convex-QP theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP permits quadratic constraints. It is convex when the objective and every quadratic inequality have positive-semidefinite Hessians and equalities remain affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Constrained Extensions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Integer-Variable Extensions
children.top_down_role: The transition from continuous convex QP to mixed-integer quadratic programming.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic matrix \(Q\) is symmetric and may satisfy \(Q\succeq0\).
At least one component indexed by \(I\) is required to be integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integrality makes the feasible set generally nonconvex, so continuous convex-QP KKT conditions do not characterize global optimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard MIQP formulation and elementary nonconvexity of integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer extension of an affine-constrained continuous QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer quadratic program has the form \[\min_x\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\le b,\quad Ex=h,\quad x_i\in\mathbb Z\ \ (i\in I).\] Even when \(Q\succeq0\), the set imposed by \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) is generally nonconvex: two feasible integer points can have a nonintegral midpoint. Therefore continuous convex-QP KKT conditions apply to continuous relaxations or fixed-integer subproblems, but do not by themselves certify global optimality for the mixed-integer problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An MIQP adds integer restrictions to a quadratic program. Those restrictions destroy convexity even when the quadratic objective and continuous relaxation are convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Variable Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The MIQP definition and the limitation of continuous KKT conditions are mathematically standard, and definition fits the extension leaf. No authoritative MIQP source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: QP Solver Procedure Families
children.top_down_role: Active-set, interior-point, projection, and iterative procedures owned by algorithm chapters.

assumptions_latex: The problem is the finite-dimensional convex quadratic program \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\;Gx\le h\}\), where \(Q\succeq0\).
The local theory concerns mathematical optimality, duality, and sensitivity statements, rather than a prescribed computational procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Active-set, interior-point, projection, and iterative solver procedures lie outside this local theory boundary.

notation.meaning: The feasible set of the quadratic program.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convex QP structural theory from solver design and implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\;Gx\le h\}\) and \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q\succeq0\), optimality conditions, primal-dual relations, and perturbation properties describe the solution set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}q(x)\). They do not specify an active-set working-set rule, a barrier parameter and Newton system, a projection operator and stepsize rule, or an iterative linear-algebra stopping test. Consequently, convergence, rate, numerical stability, initialization, and implementation claims for such procedures require separate algorithm-specific hypotheses and analysis; they cannot be inferred solely from the convex QP optimality-duality-sensitivity theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex QP optimality, duality, and sensitivity results do not by themselves specify or analyze active-set, interior-point, projection, or iterative solver procedures.
knowledge_statements.title: QP Solver Procedure Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the immutable path and role, and the mathematical statement is precise, internally consistent, and properly delimited. However, no citation supports the asserted separation between structural convex-QP theory and solver-procedure analysis. Add an inspectable algorithmic source with a specific section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: General Convex Complexity Theory
children.top_down_role: Encoding, oracle, iteration-complexity, and polynomial-time algorithm theory owned by complexity and algorithm chapters.

assumptions_latex: The input is a convex quadratic program with rationally encoded data \(Q,c,A,b,G,h\), where \(Q\succeq0\).
The local theory supplies structural optimality, duality, or sensitivity conclusions but fixes neither an encoding model nor an oracle or arithmetic-cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time solvability and iteration or bit-complexity bounds are not consequences of the local structural theory alone.

notation.meaning: Total binary encoding length of the rational problem data.
A computational resource bound depending on problem size, encoding, and accuracy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates structural convex QP theory from encoding-dependent computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational convex QP data, a complexity assertion must specify the encoding length \(L\), the accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\), the permitted arithmetic or oracle operations, and the resource measured by \(T(n,L,\varepsilon)\). KKT sufficiency, strong duality, and local sensitivity formulas alone determine none of these conventions and therefore imply neither a polynomial bound in \(n\), \(L\), and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) nor a particular iteration bound. Such conclusions require an explicitly stated algorithm and computational model. Hence general oracle complexity, bit complexity, iteration complexity, and polynomial-time theory remain outside the scope of convex QP optimality-duality-sensitivity theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural convex QP results alone imply no oracle, iteration, bit-complexity, or polynomial-time bound without an algorithm, encoding, accuracy criterion, and computational model.
knowledge_statements.title: General Convex Complexity Theory
